stem: A postoperative client who has been taking shallow breaths and moving very little develops mild dyspnea and diminished breath sounds at the lung bases. Which complication should the nurse suspect?

options.B: Pulmonary embolism identified by dull basilar percussion alone
options.C: A cardiac arrhythmia causing focal loss of breath sounds
options.D: A normal postoperative finding requiring no assessment

rationale: Atelectasis is common after surgery when ventilation is reduced by shallow breathing, pain, sedation, or immobility. Dyspnea and diminished lung sounds can occur. These findings require assessment and lung-expansion/mobility measures as clinically appropriate. A is correct. Fever is not used as a defining cue in this item.
educational_objective: Recognize postoperative atelectasis from reduced ventilation and diminished basilar breath sounds.
source_organization: National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf)
source_document_title: Health Alterations — Chapter 2 Perioperative Care; Atelectasis, StatPearls
source_locator: Common Postoperative Complications — Atelectasis & Pneumonia; StatPearls clinical features
source_claim_supported: Postoperative atelectasis can present with dyspnea and diminished lung sounds and is associated with reduced ventilation after surgery.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)

source_original.stem: A postoperative client has new mild dyspnea with reduced breath sounds at the lung bases after shallow breathing and limited mobility. The nurse should suspect:

options.A: Postoperative atelectasis causing reduced basilar breath sounds and mild dyspnea
options.B: Pulmonary embolism defined by dull basilar percussion as its hallmark examination finding
options.C: A cardiac arrhythmia that directly causes focal postoperative loss of breath sounds
options.D: A normal postoperative finding that requires no assessment when dyspnea is present

source_original.rationale: Postoperative atelectasis can produce dyspnea and decreased breath sounds, especially with shallow ventilation and immobility. Lung-expansion measures and mobilization may be used as clinically appropriate. Fever should not be used as a defining cue because evidence does not support atelectasis as a cause of postoperative fever.
source_original.source_detail: Postoperative atelectasis: dyspnea/reduced breath sounds may occur; supportive lung-expansion measures are used; importantly, evidence does not support atelectasis as a cause of postoperative fever; accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Kept the clinically sound construct, strengthened the postoperative reduced-ventilation context with NCBI nursing guidance, avoided fever as a diagnostic cue, and reduced difficulty to medium.

audit_findings.claim_audit: Dyspnea and diminished lung sounds after reduced postoperative ventilation support atelectasis.

distractor_audit.B: PE is not defined by this exam pattern.
distractor_audit.C: Arrhythmia does not explain focal diminished sounds.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: A is uniquely consistent with the presented pattern; no fever cue used.
audit_findings.blueprint: Postoperative respiratory complication fits Physiological Adaptation.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked NCBI postoperative complication table and atelectasis chapter; A remains best.
